canonical_title: A Little Something for Us Tempunauts
author: Philip K. Dick
date_display: Final Stage, edited by Edward L. Ferman and Barry N. Malzberg, 1974
card_summary: Three American time travelers — Addison Doug, Benz, and Crayne — return from history's first crewed time-travel launch only to learn, via television, that they were killed in an implosion on reentry.
page_summary:
Three American time travelers — Addison Doug, Benz, and Crayne — return from history's first crewed time-travel launch only to learn, via television, that they were killed in an implosion on reentry. In fact they have simply undershot their landing in a state called ETA (Emergence Time Activity), technically alive but scheduled to be publicly memorialized as dead, complete with autopsies, closed-casket funerals, and a national day of mourning, while the government keeps their survival classified to avoid embarrassment before a planned Soviet-style propaganda victory. Addison Doug becomes increasingly convinced that this entire sequence — the funeral procession, the interviews, the bureaucratic wrangling — has already happened to them many times before, that they are trapped in a closed time loop caused by the reentry implosion itself, and that his crushing exhaustion is the accumulated weight of having lived this same week over and over. His fellow tempunauts and the mission scientists dismiss this as depression and grief, until a Soviet chrononaut who underwent a similar crisis on an earlier mission confirms that the greatest fear of any time traveler is exactly this: an inescapable closed loop. Faced with a choice — attempt a clean reentry that might finally break the cycle, or deliberately sabotage it by smuggling extra mass (junked Volkswagen parts) into the time field to guarantee a fatal implosion — Doug, backed reluctantly by his girlfriend Merry Lou and eventually by his crewmates, chooses death, reasoning that dying for certain is preferable to risking an eternity of repetition. The story ends with Doug driving toward the reentry site at peace, having concluded that if the loop is real, he will spend eternity returning again and again to the one moment — the mourning, the flag-draped funeral, the shared national grief — that gave his life its only sense of meaning.

**Why it matters.** Dick himself rated this among his best work, telling his editor directly that he and Terry Carr both considered it 'one of my best,' and his own story note gives an unusually direct account of its origin: a 'vast weariness over the space program,' abandoned and forgotten after the excitement of the first lunar landing, transposed onto the question of what happens when the excitement of a technological program curdles into disillusionment. Crucially, Dick's note does not endorse Doug's final choice — it explicitly argues against it. He writes that Doug's wish 'to see no more summers' should be refused by the reader: 'We should individually and collectively yearn to see as many summers as we can, even in the imperfect world we are living in now.' This reframes the story's ending: rather than a validated escape into meaningful repetition, Doug's peace is presented by his own author as a seductive but mistaken surrender to defeat — 'there is nothing more defeating than a strong awareness of defeat' — that the story dramatizes as a warning rather than a resolution to be admired.

*Doug's mind returns, in his final drive, to the Kennedy and King funeral processions of American memory, concluding that all of these are, for him, 'really it was one death and one parade' — the story's closing claim that repetition and communal mourning may not be a trap at all, but the only form of meaning he actually wants.*

structure.form: novelette in four movements: return and revelation, the funeral procession, the bureaucratic decision process, the drive to sabotage
movements: Addison Doug's return to his girlfriend Merry Lou, and the tempunauts' discovery that they are believed dead by the public.
The staged public funeral procession, where Doug's visible exhaustion and impromptu remarks to reporters go dangerously off-script.
The debate among officials, scientists, and a Soviet counterpart over whether Doug's belief in a closed time loop should be taken seriously.
Merry Lou's supply of sabotage material, the crew's decision to implode deliberately, and Doug's drive toward the reentry site.
structure.point_of_view: close third person centered on Addison Doug throughout, so his exhaustion and déjà vu are delivered as lived subjective certainty rather than as a diagnosable symptom the reader is invited to doubt from outside.
structure.central_device: A closed time loop whose only available evidence is subjective exhaustion and déjà vu — the story never confirms or disproves the loop objectively, and Doug's fatal choice is made entirely on the strength of a feeling neither he nor the reader can verify.

characters.name: Addison Doug
characters.note: His conviction that he has lived this same sequence of events countless times is never validated by outside evidence, only by his crewmates' and a Soviet counterpart's willingness to entertain it — the story asks whether that is enough to justify choosing death.

characters.name: Merry Lou Hawkins
characters.note: The one person Doug trusts to help him decide, and the one who actually supplies the junked auto parts needed to guarantee the fatal implosion, making her a full participant in the decision rather than a bystander to it.

characters.name: Benz and Crayne
characters.note: Skeptical of Doug's loop theory at first, they come around not because the evidence changes but because their own exhaustion with the bureaucratic process makes death seem, on its own separate merits, preferable to continuing.

characters.name: General Toad, Dr. Fein
characters.note: Represent the state's instinct to manage the tempunauts' deaths as a media and propaganda event even as they debate, with real scientific seriousness, whether a closed time loop is actually possible.

characters.name: N. Gauki
characters.note: Confirms that he and his own mission partner shared exactly Doug's fear during their earlier, ostensibly successful time flight — the story's only external corroboration of the loop hypothesis.

settings.name: Merry Lou's A-frame house in Ojai
settings.note: The one private space in the story, where Doug first tests whether anyone still recognizes him as human rather than as a media event.

settings.name: The funeral procession on Pennsylvania Avenue
settings.note: Staged for a grieving public that believes the tempunauts already dead — restaged, in Doug's conviction, an unknown number of times before.

motifs: Déjà vu as lived, cumulative exhaustion rather than a passing sensation
A funeral and national mourning ceremony as the emotional high point of a life, sought out and returned to rather than merely endured
Media commentary (the TV anchors' scripted excitement) narrating an event whose true nature the commentators themselves do not understand
A decision about life and death made entirely on unverifiable subjective evidence, with the people closest to the person choosing to trust the feeling rather than demand proof
Bureaucratic process ('they will nibble you to death') as its own form of exhausting repetition, mirroring the cosmic loop at a smaller scale

distinctive_terms.label: Bible
distinctive_terms.note: Doug's own allusion — 'we all go to one place, as the Bible says' — reframing the loop in explicitly scriptural terms.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick left a substantial story note directly explaining the closed-loop premise's real source — his weariness with the abandoned space program — and separately rates the story among his own best.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: In this story I felt a vast weariness over the space program, which had thrilled us so at the start — especially the first lunar landing — and then had been forgotten and virtually shutdown, a relic of history. I wondered, if time-travel became a "program" would it suffer the same fate? [...] Addison Doug-One rides alive on the casket containing the corpse of Addison Doug-Two and knows it, knows he is now two persons — he is split as in a physical schizophrenia. [...] In writing this story I felt a weary sadness of my own, and fell into the space (I should say time) that the characters are in, more so than usual. [...] I felt a futility about futility — there is nothing more defeating than a strong awareness of defeat [...] Addison Doug expresses the desire "to see no more summers." We should all object; no one should drag us, however subtly or for whatever evidently benign reasons, into that view or that desire.
evidence.reading: The single most important piece of evidence for this story: Dick states outright that its real subject is his own disillusionment with the abandoned Apollo program, and that writing it left him genuinely inhabiting Doug's exhaustion rather than merely describing it. Most strikingly, he closes the note by explicitly disagreeing with his own protagonist's death wish — 'we should all object' — which reframes the story's ending not as an endorsement of Doug's choice but as a warning against it.

evidence.quote: Ballantine has my most recent story, "A Little Something For Us Tempunauts" in the current Terry Carr best s-f collection, and I consider — as Terry does — that this is one of my be[st]
evidence.reading: A direct, confident self-assessment, corroborated by editor Terry Carr's selection of the story for a best-of-the-year anthology.

evidence.quote: of Millgrove, Iowa" changed in a flash my entire conception of what a good s-f story is. So then I wrote, "A Little Something For Us Tempunauts" for Ed Ferman because I had a new mind, a whole mind again, a writer's mind, and it was set facing the f[uture]
evidence.reading: Dick crediting a specific unnamed story (title truncated to '...of Millgrove, Iowa') with catalyzing a creative breakthrough that directly produced this piece — the referenced story's full title was not captured in this evidence pass.

open_questions: What is the full title of the story ending '...of Millgrove, Iowa' that Dick credits with reshaping his sense of good science fiction just before writing this piece? Identifying it would clarify an important influence on his late style.

No secondary criticism was found for this story despite Dick's own high estimation of it and its selection for a best-of-the-year anthology — worth flagging as an archive gap for acquisition, particularly given the story's clear connections to Dick's broader closed-loop and simulated-reality fiction (compare retreat-syndrome, already read).

The story never resolves whether the closed time loop is objectively real. Is there any later interview or Exegesis passage where Dick discusses his own view on this, distinct from the story's deliberate ambiguity?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
